d: BallSocketConstraint forces its two attachments into the same position and allows them to freely rotate about all three axes, with optional limits to restrict both tilt and twist.
h:
For an overview on creating, visualizing, and simulating mechanical constraints, including BallSocketConstraint, see Mechanical constraints. Also see Roblox units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

A BallSocketConstraint forces its two attachments into the same position and allows them to freely rotate about all three axes. However, you can enable limits to restrict both tilt and twist.

Limits

You can set limits to restrict both tilt and twist of a ball socket, similar to how a human's head can tilt and turn within a limited axial range. Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the UpperAngle value to restrict tilt within a cone; it also exposes the TwistLimitsEnabled property which, when enabled, lets you restrict twist rotation through the TwistLowerAngle and TwistUpperAngle limits.

Enabling LimitsEnabled also exposes the Restitution value which defines the elasticity of the attachments at their tilt and/or twist limits.

When LimitsEnabled is enabled, orientation of a ball socket's attachments affects how it rotates. To ensure rotation occurs around the desired axis, each attachment's Axis, visualized by the yellow arrow, should point in the same direction.

kid.simple: A BallSocketConstraint pins two attachments to the same point but lets them spin in any direction, like your shoulder. You can add limits so it can only tilt so far and only twist so much, like a neck. It is great for ragdolls, swinging lamps, chains and wobbly decorations.
kid.analogy: It works like the ball-and-socket joint in your shoulder or hip, or the joint on a selfie stick that lets the phone tilt every which way.
keyPoints: BallSocketConstraint forces its two attachments into the same position.
Without limits, the parts can rotate freely around all three axes.
Turn on `LimitsEnabled` to show `UpperAngle`, which limits tilt to a cone.
With limits on, you can also turn on `TwistLimitsEnabled` and set `TwistLowerAngle` and `TwistUpperAngle` to limit twisting.
`Restitution` controls how bouncy it is when it hits a tilt or twist limit.
When limits are on, the direction of the attachments matters. Point both attachments' yellow Axis arrows the same way.

terms.attachment: A Roblox object you put inside a part to mark one exact point on it. Its Position is measured from the part's center, so an attachment at (-2, 0, 0) sits 2 studs toward the part's own left side.
terms.rotate about three axes: It can turn side to side, nod up and down, and roll, all at once, like a joystick that can also twist.
terms.tilt: Leaning away from the straight line. With `UpperAngle = 30`, the part can lean up to 30 degrees in any direction, making a cone shape.
terms.cone: The shape of all allowed tilt directions. A bigger angle makes a wider cone. 0 degrees is no tilt; 90 is a flat, wide cone.
terms.twist: Spinning around the joint's own straight line, like turning a doorknob. Limits of -45 and 45 allow a quarter turn total.
terms.restitution: How bouncy the stop is when a moving piece hits its limit. 0 means it stops dead, 1 means it bounces back as hard as it hit.
terms.Axis: Every attachment has its own arrows. `Axis` (yellow arrow) is its main X direction and `SecondaryAxis` (orange arrow) is its Y direction. With Orientation (0, 0, 0) the yellow arrow points along the part's X; with Orientation (0, 0, 90) it is turned a quarter turn to point straight up.

example.title: A hanging lamp that sways but cannot flip over
example.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local mount = Instance.new("Part")
mount.Size = Vector3.new(2, 1, 2)
mount.Position = Vector3.new(0, 20, 0)
mount.Anchored = true
mount.Parent = Workspace

local lamp = Instance.new("Part")
lamp.Size = Vector3.new(1, 6, 1)
lamp.Position = Vector3.new(0, 16.5, 0) -- top of the lamp touches the mount's bottom
lamp.Material = Enum.Material.Neon
lamp.Parent = Workspace

-- Both attachments turned so their main Axis points straight down
local mountAtt = Instance.new("Attachment")
mountAtt.Position = Vector3.new(0, -0.5, 0)   -- bottom of the mount
mountAtt.Orientation = Vector3.new(0, 0, -90)
mountAtt.Parent = mount

local lampAtt = Instance.new("Attachment")
lampAtt.Position = Vector3.new(0, 3, 0)       -- top of the 6-stud lamp
lampAtt.Orientation = Vector3.new(0, 0, -90)
lampAtt.Parent = lamp

local joint = Instance.new("BallSocketConstraint")
joint.Attachment0 = mountAtt
joint.Attachment1 = lampAtt
joint.LimitsEnabled = true
joint.UpperAngle = 30          -- can lean at most 30 degrees from straight down
joint.Restitution = 0.2        -- small bounce at the limit
joint.Parent = mount

-- Give it a push to see it sway
lamp:ApplyImpulse(Vector3.new(40, 0, 0))
explain: The mount is anchored at height 20. Its attachment is at its bottom face, 0.5 studs below its center.
The lamp is 6 studs tall, so its top is 3 studs above its center. That is where its attachment goes. The ball socket joins those two points.
Both attachments use Orientation (0, 0, -90), which turns their yellow Axis arrow to point down. Because limits are on, both arrows need to match.
`UpperAngle = 30` means the lamp can swing up to 30 degrees from hanging straight down, in any direction, but never higher.
The impulse shoves the lamp sideways so you can watch it sway and gently bounce off the 30 degree limit.

watchOut: If limits act strangely, the two attachments probably point in different directions. Make their yellow Axis arrows match.
A ball socket alone does not stop the parts from bumping into each other. Add a NoCollisionConstraint if the pieces overlap and jitter.
Twist limits only appear after `LimitsEnabled` is turned on.
